segments.source: River systems form directed networks: water has a direction, tributaries join larger streams, and upstream/downstream are relational concepts.

Silver River flows into Clearwater; Pine River flows into Clearwater; Clearwater flows into Meadow River. A canal diverts some water from Pine River to a reservoir, but the remaining flow still reaches Clearwater.
If river X flows into river Y, X is upstream of Y. Upstream relations can be followed through several confluences. Downstream is the reverse direction of flow.
Is Pine River upstream of Clearwater? Can water from Pine River reach Clearwater through the stated network?

1. Rewrite the facts as arrows: Silver River→Clearwater, Pine River→Clearwater, Clearwater→Meadow River. 2. Follow arrows starting from Pine River. 3. An arrow path reaches Clearwater, so Pine River is upstream of Clearwater.
Yes; water from Pine River can reach Clearwater.
A river network can be reasoned about like any directed network; following the arrows is more reliable than guessing from names.
Directed graph; edge X→Y means water can flow from X to Y; query reachability.
Problem 766. Crossing the fictional border network of Quartz
Political maps can be treated as adjacency networks. This lets us reason about border crossings without relying on memorized real-world geography.
Countries are represented by the fictional states Quartz, Grove, Harbor, Juniper, Fern, Linden. Shared borders: Quartz–Grove, Grove–Harbor, Harbor–Juniper, Quartz–Fern, Fern–Linden, Linden–Juniper.
Crossing one border corresponds to traversing one graph edge. A route may use only listed borders. A state is unavoidable only if every feasible route passes through it.
What is the fewest number of border crossings needed to travel from Quartz to Juniper? Is Grove necessarily crossed?

1. Turn each shared border into an undirected link. 2. A shortest-link search gives distance 3 from Quartz to Juniper. 3. Remove Grove and check whether Juniper is still reachable from Quartz. 4. It is still reachable, so Grove is not unavoidable.
3 border crossing(s); Grove is not unavoidable.
Neighbourhood on a map is a graph relation; shortest routes and unavoidable transit points are different questions.
Undirected graph; shortest path length plus reachability after deleting a candidate vertex.

Problem 771. Reading a layered map legend (A1)
A map legend translates symbols into properties. One location may have several properties at the same time.

Legend: tree=forest, wavy line=river, double line=road, arch=bridge, square=village, triangle=hill. Cells: A1 has forest, road; A2 has bridge, river; B1 has forest, river, road; B2 has road, village. Cross-domain check: researchers collected 7 reports, but 4 are exact duplicate copies that add no new independent information. Mixed-domain verification: a regional archive has 79 map sheets and receives 2 additional sheets during the exercise.

A cell satisfies the task only if it has every required attribute. Extra attributes do not disqualify it unless the task says so. For the cross-domain check, independent reports = total reports − duplicate copies. For this verification, the final number of sheets equals starting sheets plus received sheets.

Which cell or cells satisfy all of these conditions: forest, road? Explain by intersecting the clues. Cross-domain check: how many non-duplicate reports remain? Mixed-domain verification: how many sheets are available after the delivery?

1. Convert the requested symbols into the attribute set ['forest', 'road']. 2. Check each cell for every required attribute. 3. The matching set is ['A1', 'B1']. Cross-domain check: 7−4=3 independent reports remain. Mixed-domain verification: 79+2=81.
A1, B1 Cross-domain answer: 3 independent reports. Mixed-domain answer: 81 map sheets.
Map reading often means intersecting clues rather than recognizing one symbol in isolation.
Set model; each cell has an attribute set; return cells whose set is a superset of the required set.
